retrieved.snippet: The text examines various forms of consequentialism, contrasting hedonistic and preference-based theories with pluralist approaches to address criticisms regarding value, interpersonal comparisons, and demandingness. It explores indirect strategies like rule utilitarianism and satisficing models as responses to objections concerning moral obligations, rights, and the complexity of utility calculation. Ultimately, it highlights how different versions attempt to reconcile impartial maximization with intuitive moral constraints such as promise-keeping and personal relationships.

retrieved.title: philippa-foot
retrieved.snippet: Philippa Foot advances ethical naturalism and virtue ethics, arguing that morality is grounded in facts about human nature and the requirements for flourishing rather than consequentialist or noncognitivist frameworks. She contends that virtues are essential traits beneficial to human life and that moral reasoning must distinguish between negative rights and positive duties while recognizing natural norms inherent in biological functions.

retrieved.title: richard-price
retrieved.snippet: Richard Price argues that moral principles are necessary, eternal truths independent of divine will or self-interest, and that recognizing these duties inherently motivates action. He distinguishes between prima facie and actual duties to resolve conflicts, asserting that obligations arise from changed circumstances rather than mere acts of will, while maintaining a libertarian view of agent-causation.

retrieved.title: mill-moral-political
retrieved.snippet: Jeremy Bentham advances the principle of utility as both a descriptive account of human motivation and the normative standard for determining right and wrong. He defines this principle by its tendency to augment or diminish happiness, ultimately arguing that moral worth is determined by actions' capacity to promote general happiness rather than abstract rights. While acknowledging psychological complexities in individual motives, Bentham maintains that utility serves as the ultimate appeal for all ethical questions.
